E0647.summary: In a passage given in Hermes' voice, the volatile element that flies away, which sulphurs and albuminous bodies hold and detain.
E0647.body: Quoted from Hermes: sulphurs and albuminous bodies are said to be those “which hold also and detain the fugitive Ens” [I.3 ¶21]. The context suggests the term means the volatile principle that tends to escape and must be fixed.

E0648.summary: In Geber's account, what fills a fanciful soul so that it cannot receive the true intention of natural things.
E0648.body: Geber, as quoted by Atwood among the impediments to the Art, says that a fanciful soul, “because there is replete with fumosities, it cannot receive the true intention of natural things” [III.4 ¶3]. Apparently a mental cloudiness that unfits the mind for the work.

E0649.summary: An instrument of the work; Atwood says the old writers devised furnaces for every part, many misleadingly, while the true furnace is a little simple shell.
E0649.body: Atwood says the old writers devised a furnace for every part of the work, many of them misleadingly, but “The true furnace has been described as a little simple shell” [III.4 ¶38], small enough to be carried in one hand. She notes that “Geber calls this furnace Athanor” [III.4 ¶38], so Athanor is another name for it. She criticizes those who followed Geber's example and described the furnace with a misleading subtlety [III.4 ¶38].

E0650.summary: In a quoted adept's account, a transparent salt seen in the waters of the vessel, said to be no different from pumice stone.
E0650.body: An ancient and much esteemed Adeptus (identified in n26 as Grasseus) describes the waters of the vessel as “full of a certain transparent salt” [III.2 ¶25], and judges “that fusil kind of salt to be not different from pumice stone” [III.2 ¶25]. So the text equates fusil salt with pumice stone. The plain meaning beyond this is not stated.

E0651.summary: Named in a passage from Helmont that criticizes measuring all diseases by degrees of heat and cold, the method of Galen's art.
E0651.body: In the Helmont material Atwood cites, physicians are criticized for “being allured with the facility of the art of Galen” [IV.3 ¶34], that is, for measuring all diseases by degrees of heat and cold. The view is Helmont's; Galen's method is the thing rejected.

E0652.summary: Named by Atwood in a contrast: she would as soon have lived in Galileo's days as see the recovered secret sink into obloquy through modern skepticism.
E0652.body: Atwood says she would as soon have lived in Galileo's days as see the recovered secret sink into obloquy through modern skepticism [III.4 ¶12]. Galileo is used only as this point of comparison.

E0653.summary: The alchemists' name for the meadow of Divine Ideas, a place of sweet dew where Ideas descending from above are conceived and incorporated.
E0653.body: Atwood says of the meadow of Divine Ideas (the Pratum) that “the Alchemists in general call it their garden” [II.4 ¶9]. She describes it in the alchemists' words: “the philosophers have indeed a garden where the sun as well morning as evening remains with a most sweet dew” [II.4 ¶9]. In her account it is where Ideas descending from above are conceived and incorporated [II.4 ¶9].

E0654.summary: Something that, in Atwood's account, must be dissected and shorn, in parallel with stripping the Orient Animal's skin.
E0654.body: Atwood writes that “the whole garment of Light must be dissected, shorn, and the signal of victory be heroically transferred” [III.1 ¶64], in parallel with the stripping of the Orient Animal's skin. Apparently an image for laying open the vital or luminous covering of the subject. The text does not state this meaning directly.

E0655.summary: The passage at the beginning of the work through which the great change happens, which Atwood ties to the soul's willed dissolution of her bond to the body.
E0655.body: Atwood quotes the adept's cry: “O happy gate of Blackness! Cries the adept, which art the passage to so glorious a change!” [II.3 ¶37]. She equates it with the “precious death” of the Hebrews and Academics: “That was the way to "precious death", spoken of by the Hebrews and Academics, this the "happy gate of blackness" celebrates by the old adepts” [II.3 ¶37]. She also equates it with the head of Hermes' crow: “the "happy gate of blackness" celebrates by the old adepts, the "head of Hermes’ crow", which is in the beginning of the work” [II.3 ¶37]. In her context it is the soul's willed dissolution of her bond to the body, at the opening of the work. That reading comes from the surrounding passage, not from a stated definition.

E0656.summary: The common name, per Atwood, for a stage of dissolution in the work: a dark entrance with Cimmerian windings and continual terror of the Spirit.
E0656.body: Atwood describes a dark entrance with Cimmerian windings and continual terror of the Spirit, and adds: “This is commonly called the Gate of Putrefaction” [III.1 ¶58]. In context it names the stage of dissolution.

E0657.summary: In the Rosy Cross fraternity's account, the five contested stages of the work, from knowledge of the true matter to projection.
E0657.body: Quoted from the fraternity of the Rosy Cross: the work is accomplished by “entering in by five litigious gates” [III.3 ¶63]. These are knowledge of the true matter, preparation, fire to maturity, multiplication and projection [III.3 ¶63].

E0658.summary: Author of Monde Primitif, whose agricultural interpretation Atwood criticizes.
E0658.body: Atwood cites Gebelin's *Monde Primitif* to criticize its agricultural interpretation [II.2 ¶4, II.2 n3].

E0659.summary: An authority the adepts rank next after Hermes. Atwood defends his obscure recipes as deliberate veils and draws on him throughout for doctrine, the work's impediments and its terms.
E0659.body:
**Standing and veiling.** Atwood reports that the adepts rank Geber greatest after Hermes, and she defends his obscure recipes as deliberate veils [I.1 ¶31–33; works cited at I.1 n37]. In Norton's verse he is among the masters who “Wrote under coverts and Aristotle alsoe.” [I.1 ¶15]. Ripley's verse calls failed practitioners “as one of Geber’s cooks” [I.1 ¶65]. Read literally, his receipts led seekers into laboratory practice [I.1 ¶86]. From the *Summa Perfect.* she quotes his exclusion of the unworthy: “Ye sons of Avarice and Ignorance, cries Geber, and ye of evil manners, avaunt and fly from this science” [III.4 ¶18, III.4 n14]. On the word gibberish, see E0670.

**Doctrine.** Atwood uses him to support these points:
- The work is verified by experiment: “we have searched out and found, and have seen with our eyes and handled with our hands” [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n101–102].
- “All is made of Mercury” [I.2 ¶11, I.2 n12].
- Metals can be perfected: “In metals,says Geber, is lesser perfection than in animals” [I.2 ¶49, I.2 n47].
- Theory must come first: “he who knows the principles and the way of generation, which consists according to the intention of nature, is but a very short way from the completement” [I.3 n2].
- The root lies in the operator: “he has not the true root in him whereon to base his labor and intention” [II.1 ¶11, II.1 n7].
- The work fails through ignorance: “men have thought the confection of fold impossible, because they have not know the artificial destruction according to the course of nature” [II.1 ¶47, II.1 n43].
- The compound of Art is “a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur” [IV.3 ¶9].

She reinterprets his “the thing which perfects in minerals, is the substance of argent vive and sulfur, proportionally commixt in the bowels of clean inspissate earth” [I.2 ¶42, I.2 n39] as relations of the Ethereal being, not literal substances. Elsewhere he is named as celebrating the Head Stone [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n25] and as one of the Mahomedan princes who agreed about the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

**Impediments.** She follows his list of bodily and mental impediments: “Natural Impotency, he asserts, is manifold” [III.4 ¶3–6, III.4 n1]. She also follows his ranking of the unfit [III.4 ¶12–16]. His “necessary charges” she reinterprets as giving up selfhood [III.4 ¶6]. Geber gives the furnace the name Athanor: “Geber calls this furnace Athanor” [III.4 ¶38]. She faults later writers who copied him in describing it with misleading subtlety.

E0660.summary: Atwood's name for the method of the work, indicated by the order of her exposition and identified with the artistic fabrication of the Promethean Fire.
E0660.body: Atwood says the order of her exposition indirectly indicates “the genealogical method of ascent; even that artistic fabrication of the Fire which Prometheus received from Vulcan” [IV.4 ¶8]. The method is thus identified with the fabrication of the Promethean Fire.

E0661.summary: Embodied, born mortal life, into which souls descend and from whose bond and strains they must be freed. It is also the process through which every creature is brought into life.
E0661.body:
**Atwood.** Generation is the realm of birth into mortal life. Souls descend into it: “souls descending into the realms of generation” [II.4 ¶7]. They must be freed “from the bond of its earthly geniture” [II.4 ¶3] and redeemed “from the oblivious realms of generation” [II.3 ¶36]. In the work, “those strains are all finally obliterated that accede to the soul from generation” [II.3 n40]. She also uses the word for a process in which each being's central spirit is separated off: “the separation of this is constantly enacted in generation” [III.3 ¶52]. Through that process every creature is brought into life and operation. For her paired saying on generation and dissolution, see E0662.

**Quoted voices.** Crito says Intellect is withheld from every mortal nature in this life, “this however is not deprived by God but by the essence of generation” [II.1 ¶38]. Iamblicus says prayer “expels whatever is prone to generation, and retains nothing of the dregs of mortality” [III.4 ¶24].

E0662.summary: Atwood's principle that what generation binds, the inbred evil, only dissolution can unloose.
E0662.body: Atwood: “That which generation binds dissolution only can unloose” [IV.4 ¶17]. In context, what generation binds is the inbred evil. See also generation (E0661).

E0663.summary: In the later Appendix, the life into which the life-force is now wasted when it should be related to mind.
E0663.body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer of the book. There Atwood says the life-force should be directed to mind: “it is to be related to mind and not to the generative life” [APP ¶134]. In the Aristaeus story, the bees are lost along with “all the faculties of his soul, with the generative life” [APP ¶144].

E0664.summary: A power which, drawn up into intellectual alliance with the medial life and light, marks the origin of matter for the Platonists. It is alienated and later reunited to mind.
E0664.body: Reporting the philosophers' view, the text speaks of the origin of matter “when the generative virtue is drawn up into intellectual alliance with the medial life and light” [III.2 ¶9]. In a later passage, whose speaker is unclear, the primary motion of the ebbing life brings it about that “the Generative Virtue, which was alienated, becomes re- united to mind” [III.2 ¶66]. Compare generative life (E0663).

E0665.summary: The biblical book, which Atwood cites to illustrate the hidden riches of Wisdom and to liken the work to the creation of the world.
E0665.body: Atwood cites Genesis 2:10, “that land of Havilah where good gold is” [III.1 ¶8, III.1 n4], to illustrate the hidden riches of Wisdom. She cites chapter 1, “And the Spirit of God moved upon the Face of the Waters.” [IV.2 ¶30, IV.2 n19], to liken the work to the creation of the world.

E0666.summary: Atwood's term for the real, not imaginary, production of Forms in the clarified hypostasis.
E0666.body: Atwood presents the production of Forms in the clarified hypostasis as real rather than imaginary: “but as the true Genesis of Light” [III.2 ¶26].

E0667.summary: Cited by Atwood as carrying, in symbol, the tradition of the manifold powers and the preservation of the One Thing.
E0667.body: Atwood says Gentile Mythology carries in symbol the tradition of the manifold powers and the preservation of the One Thing [III.3 ¶69].

E0668.summary: Listed by Atwood as a persecuted adept and friend of Fichtuld, author of the Opus mago-Cabbalist.
E0668.body: Atwood lists George Von Welling among persecuted adepts and as a friend of Fichtuld [I.1 ¶66, I.1 ¶70]. The footnote gives his work as *Opus mago-Cabbalist* [I.1 n80].

E0669.summary: A Latin poem, its author not named here, whose fourth book Atwood quotes for the binding of a shape-changing captive (Proteus) with force and bonds.
E0669.body: Atwood quotes the fourth book of the *Georgics* (no author named) on the binding of the shape-changer. The captive held in bonds changes into varied shapes: “Verum,ubi correptum minibus, vinclisque tenebis” [III.2 ¶21, III.2 n21]. Only force and bonds compel it: “vim duram et vincula capto Tende” [III.2 ¶23, III.2 n24], and “Orando flectes: vim duram et vincula capto” [I.3 n37]. The more it turns into all forms, the tighter the bonds must be: “Et, quanto illa magis formas se vertet in omnes,” [I.2 ¶38, I.2 n37].

E0670.summary: A word that a quoted Faraday Society address derives from Geber's mysterious style. For Atwood, that style is deliberate veiling.
E0670.body: Atwood quotes an address to the Faraday Society that names Geber as the one “from whose peculiar and mysterious style of writing we derive the word geber or gibberish” [I.1 ¶33]. The derivation is the address's own. Atwood's point is that Geber's obscurity was a deliberate veil (see Geber, E0659).

E0671.summary: In Norton's verse, the vessel material that keeps spiritual matters from escaping, named as the vessel God gave. Vaughan adds that the glass is one.
E0671.body: Norton is quoted: “But other vessels be made of glasse, That spiritual matters should not outpasse” [III.4 ¶31]. Norton's Master identifies glass with the vessel God gave: “Si Deus non dedisset nobis vas Nihil dedisset, and that is glasse” [III.4 ¶31]. In our translation (by: ours), the Latin reads: if God had not given us the vessel, he would have given us nothing. The better kind of glass is called morning stuffe, and the harder kind Freton [III.4 ¶31]. Vaughan is quoted saying “the glass is one, and no more” [III.4 ¶38].

E0672.summary: Named by Atwood as one whose receipts, read literally, misled seekers into laboratory practice.
E0672.body: Atwood says Glauber's receipts, read literally, misled seekers into laboratory practice [I.1 ¶86].

E0673.summary: In a Proclus passage, an energy of the soul that faith surpasses, set beside intelligence and judgment.
E0673.body: Proclus is quoted saying faith is “which is then better than every Gnostic energy” [II.4 ¶40]. It is set beside intelligence and judgment. The term is not defined further.

E0674.summary: For Atwood, manifestations of the Demiurgic Fire made distinct in Light through Intellect, and the unities of all being. They appear as simple light, not phantasms.
E0674.body: Atwood asks: “what are all the gods but manifestations of this same Fire germinating through the projecting energy of Intellect distinct in Light?” [II.4 ¶26]. She also calls them “the genus of the gods, which are the unities of all being” [II.4 ¶29]. In her account each god is an aspect of that Fire. Intellect makes the gods visible and nourishes them. They are an intelligible union and Truth, and they appear as simple light, not as phantasms [II.4 ¶26–29].

E0675.summary: In Atwood's usage, the adepts' name for the Soul, meaning its Light, in the second conjunction. It is also the seed that must be destroyed to be multiplied.
E0675.body: Atwood gives a stated identity: “in the second the Soul, i.e., its Light; which two are, by adepts, called Mercury and Gold” [III.3 ¶30]. So Gold is the Soul's Light, predominant in the second conjunction. Its formal virtue stays sealed until Mercury penetrates it [III.3 ¶30]. Elsewhere gold must be destroyed as seed in order to be multiplied: “he that saves his gold, that is to say, remains satisfied in the first fruits of his reason” [III.3 ¶22]. Saving one's gold thus means resting content in the first fruits of reason. See also Gold Alchemical (E0676).

E0676.summary: In the later Appendix, the first conceived Paternal Light and the metaphysical seed of mineral gold.
E0676.body: This comes from the Appendix (Table Talk, begun 1860), a later layer. Atwood says: “The Gold Alchemical is the first conceived Paternal Light” [APP ¶20], and “it is the seed metaphysical of mineral gold” [APP ¶20]. Compare gold (E0675).
